newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-SPORT MOVES CLOSER TO SHOWBUSINESS AT WEEKEND.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SPORT MOVES CLOSER TO SHOWBUSINESS AT WEEKEND.

text.p: Sport moves even closer to show business this weekend in the Dutch town of Hengelo and the Canadian city of Montreal.

On Saturday Haile Gebrselassie meets Noureddine Morceli over two miles in Hengelo; on the following day Michael Johnson takes on Donovan Bailey over the equally artificial distance of 150 metres in the Toronto SkyDome.
The two head-to-head clashes are being billed as a new avenue for track and field, struggling to stay afloat in a fiercely competitive market.
They are also, though, as much a reflection of the past as a portent of the future.
More than 300 years ago, English diarist Samuel Pepys came across a foot race on Banstead Downs.
"The foot race was between Lee, the Duke of Richmond's footman and a tyler, a famous runner," Pepys wrote in May, 1663.
"And Lee hath beat him, though the King and Duke of York and almost all men did bet 3 to 4 to 1 upon this tyler's head..."
Running for money long preceded modern athletics, which did not take shape until the middle of the nineteenth century.
In the eighteenth century the British aristocracy organised head-to-head clashes, chosing one of their workers to race against the nominee of a neighbouring landowner.
Usually the runners were footmen, whose training had consisted of running beside their master's coach.
Betting was heavy and by 1820 such races were being stage for public entertainment in the larger British industrial cities.
Where big money was involved, so too was corruption and there were several contemporary reports of runners losing races they should have won.
Handicaps were introduced to make the contests more interesting, leading directly to a riot at the Lille Bridge Stadium in Fulham, London, in 1887.

A race between two of the fastest sprinters of the day, Harry Gent and Harry Hutchens, was abandoned, according to reports, because the competitors and their managers were unable to agree who should win.
The stand was wrecked and stadium set on fire by angry crowds who had laid out money in bets.
Professional racing in England came to an effective end with the 1906 Street Betting Act which outlawed wagering at sports events, although it lingered on in the north of the country and in Scotland.
Saturday's two mile race also had its antecedents in professional racing.
The first entry in the world best performances for two miles is credited to British runner James Pudney on April 6, 1852.
Pudney was one of the noted professional runners of the Victorian era and it was to be nearly 29 years before an amateur ran faster.
The first man to break nine minutes was the Flying Finn, Paavo Nurmi, who clocked eight minutes 59.6 seconds on August 24, 1931, in Helsinki.
In a further twist of fate, Nurmi was soon to be banned from the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics for professionalism, after apparently claiming excessive expenses.

On Saturday, 43 years after Roger Bannister first broke four minutes for the mile Gebrselassie and Morceli will try and run two back-to-back four minute miles. If the winner breaks the eight minute barrier he will receive a million dollars.
More than money is at stake in the trumpeted clash between Olympic 200 metres champion Michael Johnson and 100 metres gold medallist Donovan Bailey.
Both men broke the world record in their respective races in Atlanta last year and both believe they are entitled to the mythical title of world's fastest man.

To give an added edge to the race, Bailey is a Canadian and nobody who witnessed his jubilation when Canada defeated the United States in the Olympic 4x100 metres final could doubt how much beating Americans means to him.
Both men are in shape, with Johnson clocking 20.05 over 200 and Bailey running 9.99 for the 100, although neither man is the fastest this year.
Johnson, with his proven ability on the curve is the favourite, although the race will not prove who reaches the top speed.
The winner will certainly be richer. Both men will receive $500,000 apperarance money with the winner getting an extra million dollars.
